title: Claim that boxed-only intervals contain the whole -2.6 fall is false for the 1e-5 run
quote: (−0.4 to +0.7 points) have intervals (≈±3) that contain the
explanation: Table 5 boxed-only intervals are [-2.9, 4.3] (seed 1), [-2.8, 3.4] (seed 2) and [-2.0, 1.2] (1e-5, seed 0). The first two contain -2.6, but the third has half-width about 1.6, not 3, and its lower limit (-2.0) lies above -2.6. For that run the boxed-only change is therefore not compatible with a -2.6 fall (its own all-answer fall is -1.5, so the comparison is with -1.5, but the text compares against -2.6 and pools the three runs under one sentence). The sentence generalises from the two high-LR runs to all three and so overstates how little the boxed-only data constrain adaptation. The 'flat means not detected' conclusion is fine for 5e-4 but the quantitative justification is not accurate as written.

title: Identity is tautological and the boxed-share 'accounting' cannot separate drift from adaptation
quote: the fall is accounted for by the falling \boxed share
explanation: With V' differing from V only on boxed predictions, r_t = r_boxed x boxed share is indeed an algebraic identity (I checked the Table 5 numbers: 18.3/20.0 = 91.5% -> 15.7/20.7 = 75.8%, 18.1/19.4 = 93% -> 15.5/19.8 = 78%, so the quoted 91->76 and 93->78 are consistent). But because it is an identity it explains nothing: it only relocates the question to why the boxed share among correct answers fell by ~15 points. That fall is exactly what verifier-driven avoidance of \boxed would produce (writing unboxed answers escapes the defect), and equally what truncation (a quarter of the pool loses its final answer) or generic format drift would produce. The paper says the accounting 'does not exclude adaptation', yet the phrase 'accounted for' and the Conclusion's 'tied to the falling \boxed share by an identity' read as an explanation. The missing analysis is the obvious one: the boxed-share change on affected versus unaffected problems (difference-in-differences). Note also that r_boxed is never defined in the visible text, only implicitly as numerator / #boxed V'-accepted.

title: Train-on-gold is not a valid drift baseline and the paper applies inconsistent standards to it
quote: so rt drifts by about as much as
explanation: The claim is that gold-arm r_t rises (+3.3, +2.1; boxed-only +2.8, +1.7) show r_t drifts 'for reasons unrelated to the verifier'. (1) All five gold intervals include zero ([-1.2, 8.1], [-2.2, 6.7], [-2.0, 7.7], [-3.3, 6.5], and the affected subset), so by the paper's own 'flat means not detected' standard these are not detected drifts, yet they are used as evidence of drift of the same size as the self-training falls (which have equally wide intervals). (2) The gold arm moves in the opposite direction (rise vs fall), so 'about as much' is a statement about magnitude of noise, not about a baseline for the sign of the effect. (3) The gold arm is a collapsed model (49.2 -> ~17% accuracy), so the V'-accepted denominator shrinks to about a third and the composition of accepted answers changes completely; it is trained directly on reference solutions of the 350 selection problems, which are among the 500 problems on which r_t is computed. Its r_t shift therefore reflects memorisation and a changed format, not the null drift of a healthy self-training loop. (4) Table 5 does not even give gold-arm affected-problem pool counts ('—'), and the same paper elsewhere says there is 'no valid positive control' for the audit. Using the gold arm as a drift baseline and as evidence the audit is unreliable is thus partly circular.

title: 'Five re-scored runs' versus the three self-training runs in Table 5 and the 15.5-18.3% range
quote: it falls in all three self-training runs we re-scored,
explanation: Section 3.2 and Section 5.1 speak of 're-scoring five runs' leaving the decline in place and of the defect rejecting 15.5-18.3% of V'-accepted generations. Table 5 shows exactly five runs, but two are the train-on-gold arm, which declines by ~30 points for reasons unrelated to the self-training question, and whose last-round false-reject shares are 21.5% and 20.2%, outside the 15.5-18.3% range (that range is consistent only with the three self-training runs: 15.5-18.3). The text never says which five runs are meant, whether the gold arm counts toward 'the decline in place', or whether the 0.73-0.85 ratio uses gold runs. If gold arms are included, 'leaves the decline in place' is vacuous for two of five; if they are not, the five are different runs than those in Table 5 and the audit covers only a subset of them. The re-scored evidence base should be stated unambiguously.

title: The 'independent' grader is not independent of the boxed-share decline and overstates corroboration
quote: gives pass@1 changes of −3.6, −2.2, −4.6 for the three seeds
explanation: The grader is a normalised string match of the last \boxed against the gold, so any answer without \boxed scores zero by construction. The boxed share among correct answers is exactly the quantity that falls (91->76%), so this grader is mechanically sensitive to the format change at issue and cannot separate real accuracy loss from loss of boxing; it also shares the same gold labels and the same 512-token truncation. It corroborates 'same sign' but not 'the decline is real mathematics' versus 'format change'. Furthermore, 'same sign and size' is generous: two of the three pass@1 changes are smaller than under the verifier (-3.6 vs -4.8, -2.2 vs -3.2), only one of three pass@1 intervals excludes zero (and the stated power in that round is ~6 points), and the term 'stricter' is not demonstrated (no absolute levels or disagreement counts between graders are given). The grader is also available only for the final round whose recipe changed seven things at once, so it says nothing about the earlier headline null.

title: The 2.2-point 'bound' is a max over per-run upper limits that omit seed variance already shown to exceed it
quote: of about 2.2 points is the largest upper limit among observed intervals, a
explanation: The authors flag the figure as post hoc and 'not a power statement', which is honest. But it is still presented as an informative bound on possible gain and cited in the Introduction and in the claims that rest on sample accuracy. It is the maximum of upper confidence limits over many dependent runs/rounds with no multiplicity correction, so it has no stated coverage. More importantly, Section 3.4 reports that the one replicate pair differs by 3.2 points of sample accuracy, larger than 2.2, and the intervals exclude training-seed variance. A bound smaller than the observed replicate-to-replicate difference cannot be read as limiting plausible gains. It also sits beside the pre-set measures' detectable gains of 8-10 points (pass@k) and ~10 (pass@1), a 4-5x gap that a reader could take as 'the null excludes gains above ~2 points'. The sentence should be removed or accompanied by the seed-variance-inflated figure.

title: Audit is proposed as a protocol although the paper shows it has no power and no positive control
quote: expect the pressure to adapt under SFT to be weak, but we did not test this
explanation: Section 5.3 recommends check (i) as a protocol, restricted to affected problems with an accepted unboxed form, while its own numbers show 24-28 problems, 2-12 avoidance examples per round and intervals of width 10-26 points on that statistic (e.g. [-20.1, 6.3], [-14.7, 9.5]) versus point changes of -5.5, -1.6 and -0.2. No effect smaller than ~10 points could be detected, and no positive control exists (the two injected-bias runs are declared invalid). The expectation that pressure is 'weak' is asserted without evidence, while the largest affected-subset fall (-5.5) occurs in the highest-dose seed-1 run, which is at least in the direction a dose-response would predict (and the paper concedes no dose-response was run). Recommending a statistic with demonstrated zero discriminating power, without a sample-size requirement, is premature, and the claim that the injected-bias runs 'show no selective avoidance' is weak evidence given the same runs 'cannot elicit it' or lack r_t.

title: r_t is one-sided and the V-subset-of-V' assumption is never checked
explanation: r_t counts only generations accepted by V' and rejected by V. Because V' wraps the gold in \boxed{} (and the gold may contain $..$, units, or forms that parse differently when wrapped), there can be boxed predictions that V accepts and V' rejects. These do not enter r_t, yet they change the V'-accepted denominator and the boxed share. The identity is exact, but whether V' is a strict superset of V on boxed predictions is not stated. The paper should report the count of V-accepted, V'-rejected generations; otherwise r_t may understate or mis-state the false-reject rate and the claim that re-scoring with V' simply corrects false rejects is unverified.

title: Cap-share decomposition range quotes only favourable runs and sits uneasily with the Conclusion
quote: at 5 × 10−4 the cap share accounts for 12–30% of the decline in the
explanation: The check (ii) text gives 12-30% for the three original seed-1 runs and 52-72% at seed 2. According to the results (Section 4.5 as summarised), two further runs have cap shares of about -2% and 5%, and these are not mentioned here, so the quoted range is not the full spread (-2% to 72%). Together with the reported 52-72% at seed 2, more than half of the decline in those runs comes from truncation rather than lower accuracy on finished solutions. The Conclusion nevertheless states without qualification that 'At the highest rate the model is less accurate on the solutions it finishes'. That is supported in some partitions only; the sign/size of the finished-accuracy fall differs across seeds and the partition-dependent balance should be carried into the Conclusion.

title: Round-0 values in Table 5 differ between arms although round-0 draws are said to be shared
explanation: Section 3.4 says runs share exam partitions and round-0 draws. If Run A seed 1 and Gold seed 1 share the untrained round-0 generations, their round-0 r_t on 'all 500 problems' should be identical, but Table 5 reports 18.3 vs 18.2 (seed 1) and 18.1 vs 18.0 (seed 2), and the affected-parseable R0 values differ (92.8 vs 95.5, 95.1 in both seed 2). Differences may come from the 'affected' set being defined per run, or from re-sampling, but then round-0 draws are not shared as stated. This matters because the gold and self-training changes are compared as if they had the same starting point.

title: Limitations and Conclusion do not state that the final-round decline and gate failure are unattributable
quote: the gate and the bias controls one, and no multiplicity correction is applied. The
explanation: The Conclusion reports that final-round pass@1 'falls 3.2-4.8 points in all three seeds' (a detected effect, t-interval about [-6.1, -2.1]) and that the gate fails by ~32 points even with a revised recipe (2e-5 rerun: 20.6). The revised recipe changes seven things simultaneously relative to earlier rounds, so neither the decline nor the gate failure can be assigned to any single factor. A 32-point collapse when training on reference solutions at a small learning rate is at least as suggestive of a pipeline or format problem (e.g. the dollar-span shift 60 -> 1577 of 1600, fp16 training) as of a property of 'the recipe'. The Limitations list seeds and power but never says that the final-round recipe is confounded or that the positive-gate failure may indicate a pipeline defect, and the Conclusion states the null is 'for the recipe' as if the recipe were well identified. The scope claim should be narrowed to 'this implementation'.
